reckIvJxU4wRhybxA.Bio: Mario Garza is the artist and researcher behind Symbolic Studies, a project sharing symbolic insights on the zodiac, mythology, folklore and world religions, with astrology as its foundation. A lifelong artist who has worked as an art director and graphic designer for nearly 25 years, he runs Symbolic Studies from the Pacific Northwest alongside his wife Michelle, who co-hosts the podcast with him. His work traces syncretic threads across tarot, occultism and comparative religion, including the argument that the major deities of antiquity were originally polar gods before a solar model was laid over them. He also offers symbolic birth chart and tarot readings, private lessons and freelance design.
reckIvJxU4wRhybxA.Name: Mario Garza

fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Ark as the Master Allegory", "body": "Chance Garton frames the night around one image, the Ark, the Argo Navis, the Arga, the sacred ship that carries the doctrine of world ages. He argues it is the core allegory every other story can be laid over, from Adam buried in the ground to Noah floating above the flood. Dylan Saccoccio and Mario Garza agree the vessel is the microcosm and the earth itself the macrocosm, so a hero entering the cave, the grave or the boat is always the same event, the destruction and regeneration of a world, and the birth of a new era."}, {"title": "Why Dylan Says the Greek Myths Are Not Greek", "body": "Saccoccio comes at mythology through language and historicity rather than interpretation. Reading Bishop Thirlwall's history of Greece, he argues the Phoenicians reached the Aegean centuries before Homer and that the Telchines are those same navigators disguised by poetical fiction. He points to the Etruscans, whose ancestors colonized Italy, and says the artifacts that back supposedly Greek stories sit there rather than in Greece. Fallmerayer and Betham supply the harder claim, that modern Greeks are not descended from the ancients and that the Hellenes were barbarous until Phoenician mariners brought them writing, astronomy and the arts of the smithy."}, {"title": "Priestcraft as the Tool of Empire", "body": "The practical question Saccoccio keeps returning to is how religions actually spread. Not by preaching, he says, but by building a new god onto the one already worshipped, so Mercury as logos slides easily into Jesus as logos. Behind that sits an order of priests, masons, mariners and merchants moving together, because temples need astronomy and astronomy needs navigators. Garton closes the hour by reading George Faber's 1816 account of priests who personated their deities, wore the dress of women and imitated a hermaphroditic god, which he offers as evidence that church and state were never separate."}, {"title": "Eros, Eras and the Crescent Boat", "body": "Looking at an Etruscan vase showing a winged child in a ship, Garton unfolds the pun the episode is named for. Eros is fired from a bow, the bow is the prow of the ship, and the ship is the ark. Quoting Godfrey Higgins in Anacalypsis, he says the cycles of time were like men and died of old age, so every closing era demands a new Eros. The spark leaping between separated poles, Nut and Geb pushed apart by Shu, is the erotic force that regenerates the world and fathers the sacred child."}, {"title": "Where the Three of Them Disagree", "body": "Garza reads the material through the pole star, citing The Celestial Ship of the North and linking the great goddess, the arctic and the celestial mill. Saccoccio does not dismiss it, but insists that Marian pole symbolism, including the title star of the sea, is a medieval transcription rather than antiquity, and he refuses to take a position without an inscription. He is equally suspicious of cuneiform evidence surfacing only after the 1700s, alongside the Behistun inscription. Garton brokers the two, proposing that solar imagery tracks the year while polar imagery tracks the precessional cycles."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Dylan Saccoccio returns to InnerVerse to share the sacred symbolism of the supreme generative power laid up in the mythos of the Ark and the flood hero it bears. Joining us is Mario Garza, to add further observations as we explore the numerous accounts of savior-ships found across countless cultures of all ages, and what hints they may provide to our understanding of an ancient and forgotten universal empire.
